claim: Procalcitonin (PCT) has been used to guide antibiotic therapy in bacterial infections.
source: Procalcitonin (PCT) is a biomarker that has served as an indicator for bloodstream infections and has been used as a guide to antimicrobial management in sepsis and bacterial infections in the general population (ElGohary et al., 2022; Azzini et al., 2020; Kalil et al., 2016; Schuetz et al., 2013) and in cancer patients with and without neutropenia (Haddad et al., 2018; El Haddad et al., 2018; Chaftari et al., 2021b; Chaftari et al., 2021a).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research studies.

claim: Randomized trials have shown PCT to be useful in guiding decisions regarding antimicrobial therapy for lower respiratory tract infections.
source: Randomized trials have shown PCT to be useful in guiding decisions regarding antimicrobial therapy for lower respiratory tract infections (Schuetz et al., 2017; Schuetz et al., 2009; Christ-Crain et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to randomized trials.

claim: PCT cut-off values of 0.25 and 0.5 ng/ml have been adopted for critically ill patients in the intensive care unit (ICU).
source: PCT cut-off values of 0.25 and 0.5 ng/ml have been adopted for critically ill patients in the intensive care unit (ICU) (Bouadma et al., 2010), neutropenic patients (Azzini et al., 2020; Kalil et al., 2016; Chaftari et al., 2021a), and patients with lower respiratory tract infections (Christ-Crain et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Elevated PCT levels have been associated with more severe COVID-19 in the general population.
source: In patients with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), elevated PCT levels and elevated levels of other inflammatory markers have been associated with more severe COVID-19 both in the general population (Haddad et al., 2018; Frater et al., 2020; Pink et al., 2021; Ponti et al., 2020; Lippi and Plebani, 2020) and in cancer patients (ElGohary et al., 2022; Cai et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Elevated PCT levels have been associated with more severe COVID-19 in cancer patients.
source: In patients with coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19), elevated PCT levels and elevated levels of other inflammatory markers have been associated with more severe COVID-19 both in the general population (Haddad et al., 2018; Frater et al., 2020; Pink et al., 2021; Ponti et al., 2020; Lippi and Plebani, 2020) and in cancer patients (ElGohary et al., 2022; Cai et al., 2021).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Bacterial co-infections may not be prevalent in patients with COVID-19.
source: Bacterial co-infections may not be prevalent in patients with COVID-19 (Rawson et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Empirical treatment with antibiotics is often initiated in patients with COVID-19 without a confirmed bacterial co-infection.
source: However, because of the similarity in signs and symptoms between bacterial co-infections and COVID-19 and the difficulty of ruling out a bacterial infection in patients presenting with COVID-19 pneumonia, empirical treatment with antibiotics is often initiated in patients with COVID-19 without a confirmed bacterial co-infection (Rawson et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to prior research.

claim: Antibiotic overuse may lead to emergence of antibiotic resistance, undesirable adverse events, and increased costs.
source: This practice may lead to an emergence of antibiotic resistance, undesirable adverse events, and increase costs (Azzini et al., 2020; Kalil et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to prior research.
